title: Earlier one-chord experiences: Jackie McLean, Charles Lloyd, then Alice Coltrane
summary: McBee explains that struggling on a D minor tune with Jackie McLean and the long C minor vamp with Charles Lloyd prepared him for Alice Coltrane's bass line.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: You don’t concentrate, you just feel it. Something like that, by that I mean it’s just a vibe. You are now as a bassist, you are now being rather responsible to maintain the bass line that would support all that is happening beyond you melodically, harmonically, etcetera, etcetera. It was something, quite frankly, that I was already sort of familiar with. Number one my second group — my first group that I performed with in New York City was with Jackie McLean. He trained Bobby Hutcherson, Charles Tolliver, and let me see, and myself. Yeah. But there was a recording that we did, my first, my second recording in New York City was with Jackie McLean called “That’s That.” And on that record there was a D minor tune that called for you to just swing in D minor, one sound, which really caught my attention because I knew not how to fashion my quarter notes, you know, being placed at the right tempo at the right time, with the choices of various intervals and tones that would, and movement, that would not only keep the beat but, you know, provide various colorations in support of the enclave. I had no idea what that was. So I struggled during that recording. And I guess being a pretty decent music student at school I managed to play something that was reasonably accepted in D minor, right? But the very next year I joined the Charles Lloyd Quartet. And we did, we recorded “Live at Monterey” in Monterey California, a tune called “Sunrise, Sunset” where I play [scats]. In C minor. And that went on forever, the whole half of the [inaudible]. So keeping time like that I was sort of used to that when I, when I played eventually played with Alice Coltrane. But what I’m thinking is it wasn’t me that created that bass line. Alice Coltrane showed me that bass line. “This is what I want you to play.” So I was kind of comfortable with it after having made the two, mainly the one with Charles Lloyd.
